entries.title: Iceland voters reject EU accession talks
entries.summary: A nationwide referendum failed to win enough support to restart negotiations on European Union membership, despite geopolitical tensions in the North Atlantic.
entries.content:
Iceland

Iceland voters reject EU accession talks

Published August 30, 2026last updated August 30, 2026

A nationwide referendum failed to win enough support to restart negotiations on European Union membership, despite geopolitical tensions in the North Atlantic.

Icelandic voters have rejected a plan to restart accession talks with the European Union, final referendum results showed on Sunday.

The 'No' camp secured victory with 52.8% of the votes, while the 'Yes' camp garnered 47.2% support, the official count published by public broadcaster RUV showed.

The capital, Reykjavik, was the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people to support the referendum.

Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote. There was no information yet about voter turnout.

Neck-and-neck vote after long debate

Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming a member of the bloc. 

The Nordic country originally applied to join the EU in 2009 following the global financial crisis, which hit the country particularly hard.

Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a euroskeptic government took office.

Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a referendum next year but brought the vote forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.

Fishing industry pulled weight

The decision puts to bed concerns among many voters that joining the bloc would undermine Iceland's sovereignty, with fishing rights a major concern.

The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc, with 90% of industry players against the idea.

The result is a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues, including fishing and farming, to facilitate Iceland's accession.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Edited by: Natalie Muller, Sean Sinico

entries.title: Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas
entries.summary: Turkey has announced the creation of two protected zones in a disputed area of the Aegean Sea, sparking an angry reaction from Greece. Does this mark a new chapter in a long-running dispute between the two countries?
entries.content:
Greece

Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas

August 30, 2026

Turkey has announced the creation of two protected zones in a disputed area of the Aegean Sea, sparking an angry reaction from Greece. Does this mark a new chapter in a long-running dispute between the two countries?

A stint of unfamiliar calm between Greece and Turkey lasted less than three years.

After a devastating earthquake struck Turkey in February 2023 and Greece provided substantial aid, the two countries came closer together. They then signed the Athens Declaration on Friendly Relations and Good-Neighbourliness in December 2023, a further step to improved relations.

During this unusual time of calm, neither government moved to resolve long-lasting Greek-Turkish disputes, which mostly involve marking maritime boundaries. As a result, even a measure ostensibly aimed at protecting the environment has reignited regional tensions.

The latest dispute was triggered by Turkey's designation of two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean earlier this month. The park in the northeastern Aegean includes a protected area in the waters between the Greek islands of Lemnos and Samothrace. The southern park lies east of Rhodes and surrounds the Greek island of Kastellorizo.

For decades, Greece and Turkey have been at odds over the delineation of their maritime borders in the Aegean and the related economic rights, such as claims to natural resources like oil.

Greece's Foreign Ministry was quick to react to the announcement, calling the establishment of the parks "illegal." In a statement, it said the designation of Turkish marine parks in areas outside Turkey's territorial waters has no legal validity.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said at a Cabinet meeting earlier this week that he wanted to maintain good relations with neighboring countries. However, he stressed that "areas under Greek sovereignty are determined by international law" and that Greece is "always ready to defend them."

Competing to protect the Mediterranean?

For its part, Greece also announced two marine parks in 2025 — in the Ionian Islands and the southern Cyclades, both within Greek territorial waters. At the time, Turkey reacted in a clearly worded statement: "Unilateral actions should be avoided in closed or semi-closed seas such as the Aegean and the Mediterranean."

But Turkey has now declared its own marine parks — and without consulting Greece. Environmental protection appears to have been, at most, a secondary concern for the two countries in announcing their respective conservation parks. Instead, the move appears to be a new tactic for asserting dominance in the disputed maritime area — the latest chapter in a decades-long regional spat.

Greece believes Turkey sees the marine parks as a way to challenge the sovereignty of Greek islands. It fears the designation of the two parks is part of Turkey's revisionist "Mavi Vatan" doctrine, Turkish for "Blue Homeland."

Under the doctrine, Turkey lays claim to the exclusive economic zones of Greece and Cyprus — maritime areas in which a coastal state has special rights, including over fishing and the exploitation of natural resources. It also challenges the sovereignty of numerous Greek islands and islets.

Until now, the doctrine has largely remained theoretical and strategic in nature. It is now being advanced through legislative initiatives in Turkey's parliament, and Turkey intends to use the parks to formalize its claims to greater control over parts of the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.

Greece invests in defense

Greece itself is content with the status quo in the Aegean but feels threatened by Turkey, which is significantly better armed. As a result, Greece has invested heavily in fighter jets, frigates, submarines and air defense systems.

After spending significantly less on arms imports for several years, Greece ranked 19th worldwide among the largest importers of major arms from 2021 to 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Even as Athens builds new or closer alliances, Turkey is factored into decisions. In 2021, for example, the Greek government sent Patriot air defense missiles to Saudi Arabia, despite objections from the Greek opposition, to protect Saudi oil refineries from Houthi attacks — at a time when Riyadh and Ankara were at odds politically.

During a state visit with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Prime Minister Mitsotakis explicitly referred to Turkey's "destabilizing and counterproductive" role.

Relations between Ankara and Riyadh have since improved. In early August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Defense Pact, a major joint defense agreement.

An 'Iron Dome' for Greece

With Turkey in mind, Greece has also pursued strategic cooperation with Israel. Despite heavy criticism in Greece over the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza, Mitsotakis continues to maintain close ties with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The Greek Defense Ministry is planning an air defense shield over the Aegean modeled on Israel's Iron Dome. The project, dubbed the "Achilles Shield," is designed to protect against all conceivable threats — including those from neighboring countries — and is expected to be fully operational by 2029.

For now, Mitsotakis continues to strike a conciliatory tone toward Turkey. But Greece is due to elect a new parliament by spring 2027 at the latest, and Mitsotakis may face growing pressure to take a tougher nationalist stance As the election approaches.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: India's citizen-led school audits test limits of activism
entries.summary: The student-led "Cockroach" movement is taking its campaign for accountability to government schools, but the activists' methods are encountering growing resistance from authorities.
entries.content:
August 30, 2026

The student-led "Cockroach" movement is taking its campaign for accountability to government schools, but the activists' methods are encountering growing resistance from authorities.

The Indian activist movement dubbing itself the "Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)" shot to national prominence in May by leading weeks-long protests over a scandal involving highly competitive entrance exams.

The student-led campaign put the government under intense political pressure and ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July.

Now, the CJP is taking aim at India's government schools, organizing volunteer visits to classrooms, documenting conditions and demanding accountability for problems.

Launched on August 15, Independence Day in India, the campaign asks parents, students and volunteers to inspect schools and record basic facilities including toilets, drinking water, electricity, classroom furniture and school buildings. The CJP has said the findings will be used to pressure authorities to make improvements.

The initial target is to audit 100 rural government schools over two months. It has also proposed giving recognition to village leaders who improve their schools.

Unlike the first campaign, which was based on street protests, the school audits require a more sustained form of local activism. Volunteers are expected to work consistently at the local level, document conditions and follow up with officials, parents and communities.

The organization is dealing with different layers of the Indian administration. Responsibility for government schools is divided between state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies. The CJP is therefore set to tackle different rules and political interests across the country.

India has over a million government schools, according to Education Ministry data. They make up nearly 70% of all schools in the country but serve less than half of its 247 million schoolchildren.

CJP: 'We are not afraid'

That scale has given CJP a vast field for its campaign. But it has also brought a new set of challenges.

The authorities are raising questions regarding rules and locations for the CJP scrutiny, as well as safeguards when children are present.

The response is already varying from state to state. Some authorities have ordered their own inspections, while others have restricted access or taken police action against CJP volunteers.

Authorities in Maharashtra and Rajasthan states have objected to school visits carried out without permission.

In one case, a complaint by school authorities resulted in police action against CJP members after they entered the premises to conduct an audit.

In Rajasthan, restrictions have been imposed on outsiders entering government schools, as well as on filming, interviews and other forms of documentation. CJP volunteers in Rajasthan have also said they were attacked while inspecting a school.

"We are not afraid. We are seeking accountability from the government," said CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.

Officials say schools are not open spaces

In the state of Uttar Pradesh, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has ordered officials to conduct on-the-spot checks of school facilities and directed police to register cases over what he called misleading videos about schools and colleges.

The CJP has said such measures undermine public scrutiny. Authorities have said schools are not open spaces for unauthorized inspections, particularly when children are present.

Vinita Gursahani Singh, managing trustee of We, The People campaign, which works on citizen empowerment, said the limits are set by law.

"Under the Right to Information Act, any citizen can inspect schools but you need to submit an application. And that makes sense as there has to be consideration for students and teaching," Singh told DW.

"All public scrutiny is legitimate. It is our job to scrutinize. But the scrutiny has to follow process. It has to be even-handed. What applies to one citizen must apply to all," she said.

Can activists serve as inspectors?

The CJP maintains government schools are publicly funded institutions and citizens have a legitimate right to ask how they are functioning.

Its volunteers use standardized audit forms to record conditions and send their findings to the CJP, which has said it will use the material to press local administrations to respond.

But critics question whether citizen activists can assume the role of inspectors. There are concerns about whether volunteers have the expertise to assess safety or infrastructure problems and how allegations posted on social media are verified.

Mohandas Pai, an education advocate, supports CJP's focus on government schools but disagrees with its methods.

"I like young people taking interest in school education. It's a broken system, and we need reforms," Pai told DW.

But he objected to large groups entering schools and questioning headmasters and children.

"You can't just barge into a school just because you think you are entitled to do it," Pai said, stressing that "children have to have a safe, secure environment."

Pai said the CJP should instead send small teams with permission, collect systematic data, publish regular reports and use the evidence to pressure governments.

CJP spokesperson Saurav Das rejected the argument that the campaign should rely on conventional channels, saying such approaches have failed to bring meaningful change.

Responding to Pai on X, he challenged him to join the next school visit and show the volunteers how it should be done.

Questions of student privacy

The audit campaign has also raised questions about privacy, consent and disruption of teaching when volunteers enter schools, film inside classrooms or question students.

However, Kavita Srivastava, president of the People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) Rajasthan, opposes restrictions on outsiders entering schools and taking photos and videos in her state.

"Activists were visiting government schools to document their condition and demand accountability. Protecting children's privacy should not be used to prevent legitimate public scrutiny of government schools," Srivastava told DW.

A new role for the CJP

Activist Amrita Johri said the CJP's first campaign tapped into a longstanding accountability gap in India's examination system, which cost millions of young people time and money.

"The demand for accountability had popular resonance because there was no real response from the government," Johri told DW.

She backed the school audit campaign, saying public scrutiny should be welcomed.

"Public audits are an integral part of citizens' right to information and should be welcomed as an opportunity to fix accountability," she said. Johri added that the CJP needs to train volunteers, document problems and follow up with authorities to make the campaign effective.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Manhunt underway after woman killed in Swiss rave shooting
entries.summary: The shooting happened outside a rave in the northern Swiss town of Aarau. Police said they were still searching for the perpetrator or perpetrators.
entries.content:
Published August 30, 2026last updated August 30, 2026

The shooting happened outside a rave in the northern Swiss town of Aarau. Police said they were still searching for the perpetrator or perpetrators.

A 22-year-old woman has died ​after a ​shooting ​at ‌a rave ​in Aarau, Switzerland, ​police said Sunday.

Five other people, aged between 24 and 27, were wounded in the incident, some of them seriously, the police added.

A "manhunt" for the "unknown perpetrator(s)" is underway, the police said in a statement on X, adding that the motive and the exact circumstances of the incident were still unclear.

A large contingent of the Aargau Cantonal Police has been deployed and a probe into the incident has begun, the police said.

Police in Freiburg, in neighboring Germany, were also taking part in the manhunt, the German news agency dpa reported.

Meanwhile, the Cantonal police said a ‌major ​operation was ongoing and asked people to stay away from the area. They have also appealed to people to share any videos or images of the incident.

What else do we know about the shooting?

According to Swiss newspaper Blick, the shots were fired before 3:00 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) during the annual Aarauer Rave.

The newspaper quoted police spokeswoman Vanessa Rumpold as saying that the shooting occurred at the Schachen race course where the techno party was being held.

Aarau has about 22,300 residents and is located about 40 kilometers (25 miles) west of Zurich.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Nepal issues fresh flood warning as 3,000 still missing
entries.summary: Rescuers are trying to reach dozens of hydropower workers trapped in flooded tunnels, but have been hampered by further rainfall.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal issues fresh flood warning as 3,000 still missing

August 30, 2026

Rescuers are trying to reach dozens of hydropower workers trapped in flooded tunnels, but have been hampered by further rainfall.

The combined death toll from the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet rose to 750 on Sunday, with more than 3,000 people still missing, authorities said.

A fresh flood alert was issued after river levels rose again, while Tibetan authorities warned of a new barrier lake forming behind landslide debris.

Several scientists believe a glacier collapse in the Himalayas may have triggered Wednesday's disaster, sending huge volumes of water down a river valley.

What's the latest on the floods?

Nepal's disaster authority put the number killed on its side of the border at 734, while Chinese state media confirmed 16 dead in Tibet, an autonomous region of China.

Chinese authorities said the dead included over a hundred Nepalis and people from more than a dozen countries.

The Nepalese disaster agency issued a warning for fresh floods on Sunday and told residents around the Bhotekoshi River to remain on high alert as water levels rose.

Flood warning notices were sent to residents' phones, advising them to move to higher ground.

On the Tibet side, Chinese state media said monitoring drones on Saturday night had picked up a new lake forming from a barrier created by a landslide near the Gyirong border port.

Rescue teams near the Gyirong border port were moved because of the risk of the barrier bursting.

Hydropower workers still trapped in tunnels

Meanwhile, Nepalese rescuers are trying to reach more than 100 hydropower workers believed trapped and still alive in tunnels swamped by flood debris.

Rescue teams are focusing on several hydropower projects on the Trishuli River, where more than 900 workers went missing during the floods.

At one of the sites on Saturday night, army teams used drills to break into the upper part of a mud-swamped tunnel to pump oxygen and deliver a camera inside.

Nepal's prime minister's office said that teams faced "continuous rainfall and difficult conditions" but had worked nonstop overnight, "making tireless efforts to search for and rescue those who may be trapped."

Rescue effort bolstered by neighbors

Specialized teams from India and China have joined the rescue effort, along with Nepal's mountain rescue squad, which helps climbers on the world's highest peaks, including Everest.

Nepalese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said the country needed assistance in such areas as tunnel rescue, DNA testing and identifying the victims.

The US State Department wrote on X that it would provide $3.6 million (€3.1 million) in "life-saving humanitarian assistance" to Nepal, including up to three months of emergency food aid for up to 10,000 flood-affected households.

The ⁠Red Cross estimates that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Germany news: Merkel tells voters to 'stand up' for democracy
entries.summary: Former German Chancellor Merkel has weighed in on elections in Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right AfD leads the polls. Meanwhile, some politicians have called for a ban on the party's more radical state branches.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merkel asks voters to 'stand up' for democracy

Published August 29, 2026last updated August 30, 2026

Former German Chancellor Merkel has weighed in on elections in Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right AfD leads the polls. Meanwhile, some politicians have called for a ban on the party's more radical state branches.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'
  • German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches
  • Three Germans among those missing in Nepal-Tibet flood, China says
  • German firms faced a record sick-leave wage bill last year of €86 billion
  • Lower Saxony's state premier calls for deal on Volkswagen restructuring

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, August 29, and Sunday, August 30.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches

German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches

High-ranking German politicians have advocated for proceedings to ban the most radical regional branches of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, called for bans to be initiated swiftly in a joint guest op-ed in the newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.

"We once again strongly urge that proceedings to ban the party be initiated as soon as possible, with a particular focus on the AfD's clearly ethno-nationalist state branches in Thuringia, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, and Brandenburg," Pistorius and Özdemir said.

Their comments come just days before the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, where an AfD victory could result in a far-right party  leading a German state government for the first time since the end of Nazi rule in 1945.

Pistorius and Özdemir argue that it is important to distinguish between different factions within the AfD.

The two politicians say that the party's more radical, ethnically based wing rejects the constitutional principle. In their view, this wing should be subject to legal scrutiny.

They refer to this faction of the AfD as "völkisch" — a German adjective derived from das Volk, meaning "the people." The völkisch movement was an ethno-nationalist movement and precursor to Nazism. Today, the AfD is often accused of holding völkisch views because its officials repeatedly distinguish between Germans with and without a history of migration.

However, Green Party lawmaker Irene Mihalic warned against a selective ban.

"I see a risk that the idea might eventually take hold that there is an unconstitutional part of the AfD and a constitutional one," she told the Handelsblatt newspaper. "In my view, it is now clear that the entire AfD is at odds with our democratic constitution."

Skip next section British woman stabbed to death at railway station in Bavaria

British woman stabbed to death at railway station in Bavaria

A British woman was stabbed to death overnight at a railway station in the southern German state of Bavaria, police said on Sunday. 

The 31-year-old was taken to hospital but later died from her injuries.

Police reported that a 27-year-old German man was detained at the scene in Rosenheim — the third-largest city in Upper Bavaria after Munich and Ingolstadt.

Authorities are investigating the circumstances and motive behind the attack and have appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Skip next section WATCH: AfD and the battle for young voters

WATCH: AfD and the battle for young voters

For the first time since the end of World War II, a far-right politician could become a state premier in Germany.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is well ahead of the other parties, with its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, especially popular among young voters.

Siegmund presents himself as a fresh and positive figure who wants to "get Germany back on its feet."

We speak to young people in Saxony-Anhalt to find out what they like about Siegmund and the AfD.

To what extent are young people being politicized by the right? Or are they simply disillusioned with the established parties?

Skip next section Three Germans among those missing in Nepal-Tibet flood, China says

Three Germans among those missing in Nepal-Tibet flood, China says

Three Germans are among those missing following Wednesday's flash flood in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China, Chinese authorities said on Sunday.

A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were unaccounted for.

Those missing include:

  • 104 people from Nepal

  • 49 from India

  • 33 from Latvia

  • 18 from the United States

  • 15 from Britain and several dozen from other countries

"Chinese authorities have notified the respective embassies and consulates of these countries in China," state media CCTV said, citing officials.

The Nepal Tourism Board, however, said eight Germans are missing. It is unclear if the three German nationals reported as unaccounted for by Chinese authorities are included in the number reported by Nepal.

The Foreign Office in Berlin has said "a high single-digit number of German nationals" are missing in the devastating flood.

On Sunday, the combined death toll rose to 750, with more than 3,000 people still missing, local authorities said.

Several scientists believe a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas on Wednesday may have triggered a tsunami-like wall of water which swept away entire villages in the Himalayan region.

Skip next section Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'

Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called on her compatriots to "stand up" for democracy ahead of next weekend's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

The far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is leading polls raising questions about what kind of government will be formed.

Despite this, the majority of Germans are not AfD voters, Merkel said at a political event in Berlin on Saturday night.

"I believe that now, once again — something we haven't had to do for many decades — we must really fight for this democracy, simply stand up for it, be a little brave, stand by our word and say that this is a wonderful way to live," she said.

Merkel said the AfD had, to some extent, managed to "dominate all our discussions from morning to night" about politics in Saxony-Anhalt. This meant that many voters no longer knew the policies of the other parties, she said.

But while the AfD has long polled strongest in the eastern states, Merkel — who herself hails from the former East Germany — said the rise of the AfD was not limited to those areas.

"It has become a pan-German phenomenon," she said.

Skip next section German government expected to hold Moscow responsible for Leipzig drone incident, reports say

German government expected to hold Moscow responsible for Leipzig drone incident, reports say

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to officially hold Moscow responsible for the Leipzig drone incident in early August, several German news outlets owned by media company Axel Springer SE reported on Saturday.

Berlin is expected to announce the planned move in the coming days, including "extensive" sanctions, three officials familiar with the matter told German newspaper Welt am Sonntag and the media outlet Politico.

However, the three sources did not elaborate on what the specific measures could be. It is also unclear to what extent Berlin plans to hold Russia responsible for the Leipzig incident.

On August 4, a drone loaded with explosives was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which serves as a hub for military aid shipments to Ukraine for its war against Russia. 

Merz told RTL in an interview on Thursday that the federal government would soon identify those responsible for the incident.

Skip next section Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010

The total amount of wages German firms paid in sick and maternity leave has more than doubled over the past 15 years, a study from the Cologne-based German Economic Institute (IW) shows.

IW estimated that German companies paid a record-high €85.6 billion ($111 billion) in wages to employees who were out sick last year. This compares to €36.9 billion in 2010.

Of the larger figure, €72.5 billion represented gross wages, while €13.1 billion was earmarked for social security contributions.

IW said several factors have contributed to the rise, including wage hikes and inflation in other employee costs.

The institute said the total number of employed people has also grown since 2010, meaning more workers are eligible for sick leave.

IW, however, said it had noted a "significant" rise in recorded sick leave since Germany moved to electronic medical certificates in 2022.

Separate research by the Berlin-based IGES Institute in January showed that German workers now take an average of 19.5 working days as sick leave per year, a noticeable increase from about 13 days in 2018.

In an effort to stem the rise, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government will from January ban patients from receiving sick notes from doctors by phone. 

In Germany, employers are generally required to pay workers' salaries for up to six weeks before the statutory health insurance fund takes over by paying sickness benefits.

Skip next section Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring

Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring

Volkswagen's second-biggest shareholder has called on all sides to agree on a restructuring plan for the German auto giant in the next few days.

Olaf Lies, state premier of Lower Saxony — which holds 18% of VW's shareholder voting rights — said he was convinced "a viable solution" can be found.

"I strongly urge that we ​use the time remaining until the next meeting to bring the different positions together," Lies told journalists on Friday.

The state leader noted that VW must face its numerous business challenges head-on, namely costly tariffs, falling demand and intense competition from China.

But he said the group's position in Germany's industrial landscape ‌also had to be considered.

"With its sites in Lower Saxony and ‌across ​Germany, its tens of thousands of employees and their families, and its suppliers and service providers, Volkswagen also bears an enormous responsibility for the wider economy and society," Lies said.

VW's management now thinks they may need to cut up to 100,000 jobs and that several German factories may face closure.

The supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker is due to meet on September 4 ‌to discuss a ⁠turnaround ⁠plan.

Skip next section Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany

Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany

Two-thirds of residents think the United States has more influence on Germany since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House.

A poll by the Forsa research institute found that 67% of respondents agreed, while just 11% thought there was less US influence. Around 18% thought it was the same.

The survey for the German-language Internationale Politik (International Politics) magazine found only 2% of 18 to 29-year-olds and 6% of 30 to 44-year-olds think US influence in Germany is lower than before Trump's second term. That's versus 18% of respondents aged 60 and over.

Germany-US ties have soured since Trump's reelection, due to surprise tariffs, talk of seizing Greenland and open sniping over Russia's war in Ukraine and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.

Skip next section Report: Taliban team in Berlin to aid Afghan deportations

Report: Taliban team in Berlin to aid Afghan deportations

The Taliban has sent a team of three people to Germany to help facilitate the deportation of Afghan nationals, public broadcaster NDR reported.

NDR said the delegation arrived in Germany on Wednesday and is staying at the Afghan embassy in Berlin.

The broadcaster said their mission is to provide documents recognized by the Taliban in Kabul to Afghan nationals being deported from Germany.

The delegation is also due to spend time in Bonn and Munich, where Afghanistan has consulates general.

The arrival of the delegation is contentious as Germany — along with most of the rest of the world — does not recognize the Taliban government.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz calls the contacts a purely technical necessity to return people with no right to stay.

Critics, however, say his government is legitimizing the Taliban to help raise deportation numbers.

Germany suspended deportations to Afghanistan when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

They resumed three years later, initially for convicted criminals.

According to German government data, 15,343 Afghan nationals in Germany are required to leave the country, as of the end of June, including more than 1,500 children.

Skip next section AfD youth wing: Germany shouldn't leave euro

AfD youth wing: Germany shouldn't leave euro

The youth wing of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has broken ranks with party leadership and called for Germany not to leave the euro currency.

"We do not want Germany to leave the euro, but to address the existing structural flaws in the euro system," Jean-Pascal Hohm, head of the Generation Deutschland (GD) youth organization, told the Bild newspaper.

The GD is due to adopt a position on the issue at a conference in the city of Magdeburg on Saturday.

A draft statement says the euro has strengthened the European single market but has "structural flaws," and calls for reforms that would improve stability without giving up Europe's economic unity.

In its 2025 election manifesto, the euroskeptic AfD has called for Germany to leave the euro, the single currency of 21 EU member states.

The GD was established last year as the AfD's new youth organization after the party dissolved its previous youth wing, the Junge Alternative (JA), after it was labeled right-wing extremist by intelligence officials.

Skip next section Hundreds evacuated affter blaze at Berlin refugee shelter

Hundreds evacuated affter blaze at Berlin refugee shelter

A fire broke out early Saturday morning at a refugee shelter in Berlin-Spandau, a borough on the outer western edge of Germany's capital.

The dpa news agency reported that the blaze broke out on the fourth floor of a six-story building, designed to accommodate about 1,200 people

Citing the fire department, dpa said furnishings caught fire in the hallway for reasons yet to be determined.

The smoke then spread to the fifth and sixth floors.

Four people were treated for smoke inhalation, the statement said. Three were taken to hospital.

Several hundred residents were evacuated from the shelter, with between 50 and 60 people moved to alternative accommodation.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from Bonn, where the Rhine River water level is creeping back up after hitting a low earlier this month during the drought.

Overnight, a fire at a refugee center in Berlin forced the evacuation of hundreds of residents.

A report by public broadcaster NDR reveals that the Taliban has sent a delegation to Germany to help facilitate the deportation of Afghan nationals, whose asylum claims have been rejected.

Also, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) wants to leave the euro currency, the party's youth wing has spoken out against the policy, calling instead for "structural flaws" in the euro system to be fixed. 

Here you'll find our coverage of the latest news, sport and analysis from across Germany this weekend.

entries.title: Norway’s new King Haakon remembers ‘dear father’ Harald in first speech as sovereign
entries.summary: New monarch Haakon VIII paid an emotional tribute to his late father, Harald V, in his first address to the nation. Vowing to follow his own path, Haakon pledged to uphold Norway’s democracy, unity and inclusive values.
entries.content:
Norway

Norway: New King Haakon makes first speech to the ​nation

August 30, 2026

New monarch Haakon VIII paid an emotional tribute to his late father, Harald V, in his first address to the nation. Vowing to follow his own path, Haakon pledged to uphold Norway’s democracy, unity and inclusive values.

King Haakon VIII of Norway paid tribute to his late father, King Harald V, calling him "such a wonderful papa" in his first address to the nation as monarch.

"Above all, you were a person who remained committed to your values and dedicated to your duties," Haakon said Saturday in a televised speech. "We greatly mourn his loss. At the same time, it gives us consolation and strength to know that there are so many who are grieving with us."

Norway's King Harald died at 89, after more than three decades on the throne, during which time he became known as a reformer and a popular monarch. In a televised speech from the palace, Haakon praised his father as a "warm and devoted family man."

Haakon became emotional while speaking about his widowed mother, Queen Sonja. He noted that his parents would have celebrated their 58th wedding anniversary on Saturday.

Earlier on Saturday, Haakon met at the palace with leaders of the Church of Norway, parliament and the Supreme Court. He also received Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who viewed the late king’s casket after it was brought to the palace from Oslo University Hospital on Friday evening.

Flags flew at half-mast Saturday as mourners continued to gather at the palace, laying flowers alongside tributes left the previous day by more than 20,000 people.

Haakon stresses he will do things 'his own way'

Haakon said he would follow his own path, as his father did before him, while reaffirming the principles of Norway’s constitutional monarchy. He is due to swear an oath in parliament on Tuesday to uphold the country’s constitution and laws.

"We believe in our system of self-governance — and in democracy. We believe in a society built on the rule of law, where every individual has equal worth," he said.

Haakon automatically became king following his father’s death. Norway does not hold coronations, which were abolished by parliament in 1908.

But, like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906.

The Norwegian prime minister told Reuters news agency that Haakon shared many of his father’s qualities, particularly his "ability to create an atmosphere of togetherness."

Mourning and challenges for the royal family

A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet set for Harald’s funeral. Churches across Norway will hold memorial services Sunday, including one in Asker, south of Oslo, which the royal family was scheduled to attend.

Harald was widely regarded as a symbol of an open and tolerant Norway and praised for leading a modern, modest monarchy.

The king had been hospitalized in Oslo since August 17 with hemolytic anemia, a condition that causes the rapid destruction of red blood cells and can lead to fatigue and shortness of breath. His health had deteriorated in recent years, forcing him to reduce his official duties.

The royal family has also faced a series of challenges. Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, has come under scrutiny over her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

In June, her son from a previous relationship was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes, a sentence he is appealing.

Mette-Marit, 53, who has a serious lung disease, underwent a lung transplant in July.

entries.title: Turkish, Somali forces free vessel seized by pirates in Somalia
entries.summary: Turkish and Somali forces have freed the MV LUTUF after pirates hijacked the vessel off the coast of Somalia. The 10-day operation killed 14 alleged pirates and destroyed four boats used by the attackers.
entries.content:
August 29, 2026

Turkish and Somali forces have freed the MV LUTUF after pirates hijacked the vessel off the coast of Somalia. The 10-day operation killed 14 alleged pirates and destroyed four boats used by the attackers.

Turkey’s navy and Somali armed forces have freed a hijacked vessel in Somali waters and killed 14 alleged pirates following a battle that lasted several days, Somalia’s government said on Saturday.

"During the 10-day operation, four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed," said a Somali Defense Ministry statement. "The sustained military pressure finally forced the remaining pirates to abandon the ship."

The MV LUTUF, a Cameroon-flagged vessel, was hijacked on August 17 off the coast of the Nugaal region of Puntland state. The joint Turkey-Somalia operation was carried out as part of a defense cooperation agreement between the two countries.

The ministry did not provide details about any casualties or the well-being of the crew aboard the vessel but said, "The forces subsequently secured the MV LATUF, which has now safely resumed its journey."

According to AFP news agency sources, at least eight members of the crew were on board, including one Turkish national.

Resurgence of piracy along Somalia’s coast

The Horn of Africa has seen a resurgence in piracy since April, according to figures from the International Maritime Organization, with at least 15 attacks off the coast of Somalia this year.

At least five cargo ships were held hostage, the most recent of which was seized on August 20 off Yemen.

These attacks are the highest since 2013. Piracy was rampant  off the coast of Somaliain the 2000s. It peaked in 2011 before being curbed by international naval deployments and new protection measures for commercial shipping.

The resurgence of piracy in the Horn of Africa is adding to mounting challenges for international shipping in the Middle East, where vessels are already navigating around the contested Strait of Hormuz and seeking to avoid Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.

In recent years, pirate attacks have also increased along the West African coast, adding another layer of risk for commercial shipping.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinian homes in West Bank
entries.summary: Masked Israeli settlers launched their first major attack since initiating a siege in the village of Qusra earlier this month. Saturday's attacks were met with rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
entries.content:
Middle East

Israeli settlers attack Palestinian homes in West Bank

August 29, 2026

Masked Israeli settlers launched their first major attack since initiating a siege in the village of Qusra earlier this month. Saturday's attacks were met with rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, pelting them with rocks and trapping residents in their homes.

The incident was the first major attack by Israeli settlers since they began a siege in the villages of Qusra and neighboring Jalud earlier this month.

On Saturday, settlers descended on Qusra and began pelting Palestinians with rocks. When dozens of residents sought to barricade themselves in a home, settlers followed them in, according to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).

"The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside the house," said an IDF statement.

Who is the IDF protecting in such situations?

Although the IDF said settler vehicles had been impounded and authorities were gathering evidence, Palestinian media said the IDF protected the settlers during the melee.

A number of Palestinians said they were injured after being pepper sprayed by settlers, and reported that other Israeli settlers had tried to burn nearby fields owned by Palestinians.

One Palestinian said the IDF had fired tear gas into the home that he was in and held several people inside while at the same time letting Israeli settlers go free.

Other Palestinians said IDF officers had handcuffed, blindfolded and beaten residents trapped inside before letting them go.

Local Palestinians told international news teams that they had been trapped in their homes for hours waiting for help from the IDF.

The IDF did not comment on the use of tear gas nor accusations of handcuffs and beatings.

Saturday attacks elicit rare criticism from Netanyahu

Saturday's attacks took place just yards away from three other Qusra homes that radical Jewish settlers targeted in a siege that began three weeks ago.

Despite a massive Israeli military presence that local Palestinians say has kept them imprisoned in their houses, residents report near-daily settler encroachments.

Rights groups say settler aggression is part of an — illegal — effort to seize land from residents in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians hope to one day found their own independent state. The Israeli government has rejected accusations of illegality. Various Israeli political figures have justified the settlements for security reasons or argued there are biblical grounds for the creation of the settlements.

The IDF has said it will continue "to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area."

Although settlers have been emboldened by the stance of Israel's far-right government — which has encouraged settlement building despite broad international opposition — the Saturday attack managed to elicit rare criticism from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

On Saturday, Netanyahu released a statement on X saying, "I strongly condemn the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud by a handful of rioters who are violating the law, causing a grave injustice to the law-abiding Jewish community, interfering with the IDF in carrying out its missions, and harming Israel's standing in the world."

Increasing Israeli settler violence has even garnered criticism from US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who recently denounced radical settlers in the West Bank as "Israeli terrorists," adding that those behind the siege of Qusra could face US sanctions.

entries.title: Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27
entries.summary: Dozens of people were killed when a minibus carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck in central Zimbabwe. The crash near the town of Chivhu is the latest deadly road accident in the African country.
entries.content:
Africa

Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27

August 29, 2026

Dozens of people were killed when a minibus carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck in central Zimbabwe. The crash near the town of Chivhu is the latest deadly road accident in the African country.

At least 27 people were killed in a minibus crash in central Zimbabwe after the vehicle carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck, police said Saturday. Seven people were injured.

Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said members of a popular Indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling to a conference on Friday when their minibus collided with a truck on a major highway near the town of Chivhu, about 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare.

The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus. Both vehicles were carrying an "unspecified" number of passengers, Nyathi said in a statement.

Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell.

Zimbabwe faces road safety crisis

Authorities say 94% of road accidents occur due to human error. Many Zimbabweans rely on privately operated minibus taxis, known locally as kombis, for everyday transportation. The vehicles are often criticized for carrying more passengers than allowed.

Zimbabwe’s roads are also riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect, while driving standards can be poor.

In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in southern Zimbabwe. Earlier that month, a woman and her five children were killed when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa.



Road crashes kill about 300,000 people across Africa each year, accounting for roughly a quarter of the global road death toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate, the commission says.

This is despite Africa’s 1.5 billion people accounting for only about 3% of the world’s vehicle fleet.
